lessons.title: la tête — "the head"
lessons.gloss: the head — from Latin for a clay pot

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: The first body part, and one of the best etymologies in French. The word for head is not the Latin word for head.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The word

segments.text: la tête — the head. Feminine, so la.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: Latin had a perfectly good word

segments.text: Latin's word for "head" was caput. You can see it surviving all over Europe:

French has caput too, and in two layers. Inherited, worn down by use: chef ("chief," originally "head"), chapitre, cap (a headland), achever ("to finish" — to bring to a head). Re-borrowed later, straight from written Latin: capital, capitaine, décapiter.
What French does not use it for is the thing on your shoulders.
Tête comes from Latin testa: an earthenware pot, a shell, a potsherd.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: Why a pot?

segments.text: Soldiers' slang. Roman troops called the skull a testa the way English speakers say someone got hit on the noggin — a noggin being a small mug. It was a joke, it spread, and eventually the joke replaced the real word in Gaul and Italy.
So a French speaker saying j'ai mal à la tête is, historically, saying "my pot hurts."
Testa is still visible in English test — which began as the shallow pot an alchemist used to assay metals.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: The circumflex is a receipt

segments.text: Look at the accent: tête. Chapter W01 taught what a circumflex records — a letter that used to be there, almost always an s.
testa becomes Old French teste becomes modern tête.
The s stopped being pronounced, and the accent was put in to mark the grave. That is why English, which borrowed from Old French before the s fell, still has it in test.

segments.instruction: "j'ai mal à la tête" — "my head hurts"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "j'ai mal à la tête" — "my head hurts"]

segments.text: Say "the head." (La tête — feminine.) Does it come from Latin caput? (No — from testa, an earthenware pot.) Why a pot? (Roman soldiers' slang for the skull, which replaced the proper word.) Where did caput survive in French? (Inherited in chef, chapitre, cap, achever; re-borrowed in capital, capitaine, décapiter — just never for the head itself.) What does the circumflex on tête record? (A lost s — teste, still visible in English test.) Next: the hand.

lessons.title: la main — "the hand"
lessons.gloss: the hand — feminine despite ending in a consonant, and the root of half the words you know

segments.text: Where tête abandoned its Latin ancestor, this one kept it — and then lent it to English several dozen times over.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The word

segments.text: la main — the hand. Feminine, and worth flagging: it ends in a consonant and still takes la. French gender is not predictable from the ending, which is why this book always gives you the article.
The -ain is the nasal vowel from Chapter 11's pain — say them together: pain, main.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: manus in English

segments.text: Main comes from Latin manus, "hand." That word is inside an enormous number of English words, and once you see it you cannot unsee it:

utterances: English: manual. literally: done by hand.
English: manufacture. literally: made by hand (manus + facere "to make").
English: manuscript. literally: written by hand (manus + scrībere).
English: maintain. literally: hold in the hand (manū tenēre).
English: manage. literally: to handle — via Italian maneggiare, of horses.
English: manoeuvre. literally: work by hand (manū operārī).

segments.text: Manufacture is the one worth pausing on. It means "made by hand" — and it now names precisely the thing that isn't.

blocks.title: The phrase, taken apart: French kept it too

segments.text: Maintenir / English maintain is Latin manū tenēre, "to hold in the hand" — a hand, plus the verb tenēre, "to hold."
So maintenance — the least romantic word in any office — is literally keeping something in hand.

segments.instruction: the family — "manual, manuscript, maintain — all a hand"

[YOU SAY: the irony — "**manufacture** = made by hand"]

segments.text: Say "the hand." (La main — feminine, despite the consonant ending.) What Latin word is it from? (Manus.) Give three English words built on it. (Manual, manufacture, manuscript, maintain, manage, manoeuvre.) What does manufacture literally mean? ("Made by hand" — now the name for the opposite.) And maintenir? (Manū tenēre, "hold in the hand".) Next: the rest of the body.
